content: Developing and validating effective strategies, as well as introducing new drugs to interrupt the natural progression of diseases before patients reach the hospital, has the potential to save thousands of lives annually and reduce the incidence and severity of long-term complications. Investment in research focused on pre-hospital treatment, including first aid and therapeutic interventions, will enhance outcomes. Additionally, improving health care-seeking behavior is critical, as in many snakebite-affected communities, 60–80% of victims rely on traditional medicine or spiritual healers, often with poor results. To address this, it is essential to understand the factors influencing these treatment decisions and investigate why such choices persist in communities. Engaging with traditional medicine practitioners and influential community members to encourage better health care-seeking behavior or to act as first responders can lead to increased use of allopathic medicine and improved outcomes. Operational research into the socio-cultural, economic, and spiritual factors affecting snakebite envenoming outcomes is vital, as these influences vary significantly across different contexts and cultural dynamics. Identifying issues contributing to poor outcomes, such as pre-hospital mortality, chronic morbidity, and substantial economic losses, will enhance the specificity and success of local programs. Ensuring the safety, quality, and effectiveness of antivenoms requires modernization of all production phases, including the collection of snake venoms. Access to high-quality antivenoms and other necessary medical treatments is essential for successful recovery from snakebite envenoming. However, the lack of effective antivenoms in regions such as sub-Saharan Africa and South/Southeast Asia is a major contributor to high mortality and disability rates among snakebite victims. Strategic investment is urgently needed to improve the production, regulation, and supply of antivenoms, foster collaboration between industry and academia, and stabilize fragile markets. Emerging technologies may revolutionize snakebite treatment, and investment in research to develop next-generation therapies is crucial. Beyond antivenom, victims often require additional medical care tailored to the specific circumstances of their case, such as the type of snake involved, the time elapsed since the bite, and the severity of envenoming. Innovative research to optimize and rationalize snakebite treatment protocols is essential to improve outcomes. Advances in medical treatment and management of long-term physical and psychological sequelae are possible but require investment in clinical research and its translation into practice. Prioritizing clinical trials for antivenoms, medical interventions, and drug combinations will generate evidence to inform clinical guidelines and protocols, which can be integrated into national health worker training programs. Strengthening health systems to provide comprehensive snakebite management will benefit all patients, not just those affected by snakebites. Health worker training in diagnosing and treating snakebite envenoming is often inadequate, with limited opportunities for professional development. Integrating locally relevant training packages into health worker curricula at all levels will improve clinical competence and patient outcomes. Regular in-service training for rural health workers is particularly important, as their skills in managing snakebite envenoming often overlap with broader clinical practices. Standardized treatment protocols and clinical tools will enhance decision-making, improve outcomes, and allow for reliable data analysis and comparison. Point-of-care diagnostic tests for snakebite envenoming need to be more accurate and reliable to reduce treatment delays and improve patient outcomes. Post-acute care and rehabilitation services for snakebite victims with disabilities have been neglected and should be included in treatment pathways to accelerate recovery and reintegration into productive life. Comprehensive management protocols, training curricula, and clinical tools will be developed to improve treatment and recovery for snakebite patients. Snakebite envenoming is a serious medical emergency, yet many health systems lack the resources, personnel, and infrastructure to manage it effectively. Strengthening health systems, including disease surveillance, regulatory frameworks, and well-equipped facilities, will improve outcomes for all diseases, including snakebite. The high costs of antivenom and associated treatments often drive families into poverty, particularly in countries like India and Bangladesh. Initiatives to defray these costs, such as making treatment free or including snakebite envenoming in health insurance schemes, will encourage more victims to seek medical care, resulting in better outcomes and reduced financial hardship. Improving access to essential medicines, medical products, and consumables will advance progress toward universal health coverage by 2030. Research into the economic costs of snakebite envenoming and financing models will inform policies to reduce the financial burden on affected families. Strengthening rural primary health care services and ensuring access to life-saving interventions, including antivenom, will improve initial treatment and outcomes. Investment in infrastructure, transport, and communication systems will enhance access to health care for all citizens. Innovative systems for procurement, distribution, and surveillance of antivenoms are needed to address logistical challenges in remote rural communities. Research into emerging technologies, such as portable cold chains and mobile surveillance tools, will support the implementation of effective interventions. Prequalification will help regulatory agencies and organizations procure high-quality medicines, restoring confidence in antivenoms and stabilizing markets. Encouraging partnerships between academia and industry will foster innovation and improve the production, quality control, and testing of antivenoms. By 2030, new therapeutic candidates and next-generation treatments will be developed to address the current supply crisis and improve outcomes for snakebite victims worldwide.
